name: printf Format Checker
blurb: whether a format string matches its argument types
intro: Finds the printf-style calls in pasted C code and checks every conversion against its argument's type after the default argument promotions, using the integer sizes and stdint typedefs of the chosen target (uint32_t is unsigned long on arm-none-eabi but unsigned int on Linux). Types come from the declarations in the code, a declarations box, casts and literals; an argument can also be written as a bare type name.

inputs.label: Code with printf calls
Declarations (optional)
inputs.help: Variables, prototypes and typedefs the code uses but does not declare, e.g. 'typedef uint32_t tick_t;'.

inputs.label: Extra printf-like functions
inputs.help: name:index of the format argument (0 = first).

examples.title: STM32 debug prints with uint32_t and size_t

input.code:
printf("%d %lu %s %f", uint64_t, size_t, const char *, float);
printf("%x %p", uint32_t, int *);

usage: Give C code containing printf/fprintf/snprintf/printk/ESP_LOGx/LOG_INF calls (arguments may be expressions or bare type names like uint32_t), optional declarations, the target (arm, ilp32, lp64, llp64, avr) and optional extra function names as name:formatIndex. It returns a table of every conversion with its argument, inferred type, expected type and verdict (ok / note / warning / error) with the specifier to use, counts, and a Problems text. Use it to review log statements before porting code between targets or to explain -Wformat warnings.
sources: ISO/IEC 9899:2011 7.21.6.1 (fprintf conversions and length modifiers), 6.5.2.2p6 (default argument promotions), 6.3.1.8 (usual arithmetic conversions), 7.8.1 (inttypes.h PRI macros)
GCC manual: -Wformat, -Wformat-signedness, -Wformat-security; target type sizes from GCC's __INT32_TYPE__ etc. per target
newlib-nano and avr-libc documentation (float printf needs -u _printf_float / -lprintf_flt)
